Course Overview
This site contains the teaching material for BVS1 – Betriebssysteme at TH Köln, ICCT, for Winter Semester 2026/2027 · TH Köln · ICCT. The course is attended by students from multiple Bachelor programmes.
The course provides two aligned representations: concise lecture-specific Beamer slides for classroom interaction, and a reader-oriented chapter source used for both the PDF script and the HTML course.

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
text:
1.1 One program can run without a guest operating system
An operating system is familiar enough that it is easy to begin with examples rather than with the problem it solves. Windows, Ubuntu, Android and macOS are recognizable operating-system environments, but naming familiar systems does not yet explain why operating systems exist.
BVS1 therefore starts with a smaller question:
The first practical system is deliberately tiny. We use QEMU to provide a machine with an RV64 (64-bit RISC-V) CPU. This is our target: the machine for which we build the program. It runs one program and prints:
The experiment gives us a concrete machine to reason about before we introduce operating-system mechanisms.
At the lowest level, a processor executes instructions. Those instructions operate on registers and memory and can communicate with devices.
One important idea of the stored-program / Von Neumann model is that instructions and data are both kept in memory.
A deliberately simplified machine model is:
This model omits many details of real hardware, but it is enough for the first distinction:
The point here is conceptual rather than historical or microarchitectural. Modern processors may use separate instruction and data caches internally, but the important point here is that instructions and data both occupy target memory. Lecture 2 returns to this idea and makes the abstract memory model concrete.
In the Hello BVS1 experiment, QEMU provides the target machine. The target contains an RV64 CPU, memory and devices. The program is loaded and begins executing without a guest operating system.
The physical computer still runs an operating system, and our Ubuntu development environment also runs an operating system. The important observation concerns the target:
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
text:
instructions + data
             │
             ▼
          memory
             ▲
             │
             ▼
            CPU
             │
             ▼
          devices


CPU, memory and devices exist independently of an operating system.





Executing instructions is not, by itself, what makes an operating system necessary.


1.1.1 Interpreting the experiment
The classroom experiment deliberately separates observation from explanation. Consider these statements:

QEMU executed our program.
A virtual CPU executed our program.
Ubuntu executed our guest program.
The target had an operating system.
QEMU was already running before our guest program started.
The string Hello BVS1 existed somewhere in memory while the program was running.

The purpose of discussing them is to expose the execution model.
A precise description is:

the Ubuntu development VM runs the QEMU process;
QEMU implements the target machine;
the target contains an emulated RV64 CPU, memory and devices;
the RV64 program runs on that target;
the target has no guest operating system.

Saying “QEMU executed the program” is understandable in informal language, but the more useful model is that QEMU emulates the machine whose CPU executes the target instructions.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
section: 1.2 The ISA connects software and processor
text:
1.2 The ISA connects software and processor
Machine code only has meaning if software and the processor agree on what each instruction means.
This agreement is the Instruction Set Architecture (ISA).
An ISA specifies properties visible to machine-level software, including:

instructions and their encodings,
registers,
memory-addressing rules,
exceptional control transfers,
privilege mechanisms.

Different processor implementations can implement the same ISA.
The ISA should therefore be distinguished from the microarchitecture:

ISA: the contract visible to software;
microarchitecture: how a particular processor implements that contract internally.

For BVS1, the teaching target uses RV64, the 64-bit form of RISC-V.

1.2.1 Why RV64?
RISC-V is a teaching choice, not a claim that it is the best ISA for every system.
It offers a comparatively regular architecture, public specifications, a modern privilege model, suitable development tools, and a well-supported QEMU virt machine. These properties let us expose operating-system mechanisms without making historical processor complexity the subject of the course.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
section: 1.3 Development host and target are different roles
text:
1.3 Development host and target are different roles
The machine on which software is developed does not need to use the same ISA as the machine for which the program is built.
In BVS1:

the development host is the Ubuntu bvs1 VM in which the development tools run;
the target is the RV64 machine for which we build the program.

The development VM may itself run on an x86-64 or Arm64 host platform. The teaching target is nevertheless RV64.
This gives two separate questions:

Where do the development tools execute?
Which machine will execute the generated program?

Keeping these roles separate will matter when we build code on one machine for another and when we examine emulation.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
text:
1.4 Virtualization and emulation are different
The most useful first question is:

Can the physical CPU execute the guest or target instructions directly?

That question separates the roles of virtualization and emulation more clearly than the word virtual machine by itself.

1.4.1 Virtualization: the guest instructions already belong to the host ISA
In hardware-assisted virtualization, guest and host normally use the same processor ISA.
A guest instruction is therefore, in the ordinary case, already an instruction that the physical CPU understands. Most non-privileged guest instructions can execute directly on the physical processor.
The virtualization mechanism controls the parts that must not simply be handed to the guest, for example:

isolation between machines,
privileged processor state,
access to memory and devices,
transitions that require intervention by the virtualization layer.

A simplified model is:
guest instruction
       ↓
physical CPU
The important point is not that virtualization performs no mediation. It is that the guest machine does not require a different instruction vocabulary from the physical CPU.
In BVS1, Multipass manages the Ubuntu development VM using virtualization facilities available on the host platform. The exact backend can differ between operating systems.


1.4.2 Emulation: the target instruction may not be a host instruction
Emulation can reproduce a machine whose ISA differs from the host ISA.
Suppose the physical processor uses x86-64 while the BVS1 target uses RV64. The physical x86-64 CPU does not directly understand an RV64 instruction.
An emulator must therefore reproduce the effect of the target instruction. Conceptually:
RV64 target instruction
          ↓
        QEMU
          ↓
interpret / translate
          ↓
host operations
          ↓
physical CPU
The word interpret is useful for the conceptual distinction, but it should not be understood as a claim that an emulator must process every instruction individually. QEMU can dynamically translate blocks of target instructions into host code.
The essential point is:

Virtualization can largely run guest instructions directly; emulation must reproduce what target instructions would do when the host cannot execute them directly.



1.4.3 Our BVS1 machine stack
The resulting stack is:
physical host
     ↓  virtualization (managed through Multipass)
Ubuntu development VM: bvs1
     ↓  runs
QEMU
     ↓  emulates RV64
RV64 target machine
     ↓  executes
Hello BVS1
The layers have different roles:

the physical host provides the real CPU, memory and devices;
the Ubuntu development VM is the common environment in which the course tools run;
Multipass manages that development VM and is not an additional machine layer;
QEMU runs as a normal program inside the development VM;
QEMU emulates the RV64 target machine;
Hello BVS1 executes on that target.

Only the RV64 target is the teaching machine whose operating-system mechanisms we will build. It initially contains no guest operating system.
A virtual machine is the machine environment presented to software. Virtualization and emulation are different techniques that can provide such environments.
QEMU itself is capable of more than the configuration used here: in other settings it can also participate in hardware-assisted virtualization. In BVS1, its relevant role is RV64 emulation.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
section: 1.5 The toolchain connects development host and target
text:
1.5 The toolchain connects development host and target
The source program is written in a human-readable programming language, but the target CPU needs RV64 machine instructions.
The toolchain is the set of cooperating build tools. The compiler and assembler translate source into target machine code. They produce object files: target-specific intermediate files that still need to be combined. The linker combines those objects and resolves references between them.
These build products use ELF (Executable and Linkable Format), a binary format used here for both object files and the final executable.
A simplified build path is:
source code
    ↓
cross compiler / assembler
    ↓
object files
    ↓
linker
    ↓
RV64 executable
    ↓
QEMU
    ↓
RV64 target machine
A cross compiler runs on one architecture while producing code for another target architecture. This is cross-compilation.
QEMU has a different role: it does not translate source code into the executable. It provides the machine on which the already generated target program can run.

1.5.1 Object files are not yet the complete program
Compilation and assembly can already produce target-specific object files. These can contain RV64 machine code, but they are not yet the complete executable. Separate pieces still have to be combined and references between them resolved.
The final result of this build path is a linked RV64 ELF executable that QEMU can load for the target machine.
Lecture 2 unfolds this path manually: we inspect the object files, discover what is still unresolved, and then see why linking and the target memory layout are necessary.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
section: 1.6 When does an operating system become useful?
text:
1.6 When does an operating system become useful?
The Hello BVS1 target can run one tiny program without a guest operating system.
Now change the requirement:

The machine must run two programs.

New questions immediately appear:

Which program receives the processor?
Where is each program’s state kept?
What happens when one program waits for a device?
Can one program overwrite another program’s memory?
Who coordinates access to shared devices?
How does a program request a shared service?

Increase the requirements further:

many programs,
multiple users,
persistent storage,
keyboard and display,
networking,
failures,
programs that do not trust one another.

The problem is no longer merely “execute instructions”.
Now the system needs mechanisms for sharing, coordination, protection and abstraction.
This gives us the working definition used in BVS1:

An operating system is software that helps turn hardware into a usable computer system by providing abstractions, resource management, coordination, protection, and services for programs and users.

This is intentionally a working definition.
We will test and sharpen it as concrete mechanisms are introduced.
Two classical viewpoints are already visible:

Operating system as resource manager
CPU time, memory, storage and devices are finite resources that must be shared and controlled.
Operating system as abstract machine
Programs should not need to manipulate every hardware detail directly. The operating system can provide safer and more useful abstractions and services.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
text:
1.7 Applying the working definition
The opening lecture deliberately asks students to classify several familiar terms before the working definition is established.
After deriving the definition, the distinctions become clearer:

Windows, Ubuntu and Android are complete operating-system environments.
The Linux kernel is the core used by Linux-based operating-system environments, not such an environment by itself.
UEFI is firmware and a firmware interface/environment.
QEMU is an emulator and virtualizer.
Docker provides container tooling built on operating-system mechanisms.
Firefox is an application.

The purpose of the exercise is not to memorize labels.
It is to ask which responsibilities a component actually assumes and at which layer it operates.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
section: 1.8 From Hello BVS1 to a minimal operating system
text:
1.8 From Hello BVS1 to a minimal operating system
The course deliberately starts with a target that can do very little:
Hello BVS1
The semester question is:

What must we add to Hello BVS1 before we would call the result an operating system?

Initial answers may include:

handling devices,
multiple executions,
scheduling,
protection,
memory management,
system services,
communication,
persistent storage,
users,
a command interface.

At the beginning these are hypotheses, not a checklist to memorize.
We add mechanisms only when a new requirement gives us a reason for them.
The practical target remains:

a small educational operating system on RV64 and QEMU virt, eventually providing a simple shell

The red thread is:
a machine executes code
    ↓
software communicates with devices
    ↓
events must be handled
    ↓
multiple programs must coexist
    ↓
programs compete for the CPU
    ↓
programs and resources need protection
    ↓
programs need operating-system services
    ↓
programs need coordination
    ↓
programs need communication
    ↓
a user needs to control programs
    ↓
a simple shell
The course is therefore not organized as a catalogue of terminology.
Each new mechanism should answer a problem that the current system has acquired.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems
text:
1.9 Key ideas
Lecture 1 establishes a small number of distinctions that we will use repeatedly:

A target processor can execute a program without a guest operating system.
CPU, memory and devices exist independently of the OS.
An ISA defines the machine-level contract on which software relies.
Development host and target are different roles.
Virtualization and emulation are different techniques.
Multipass gives us the virtualized development environment; QEMU emulates our RV64 target in the BVS1 setup.
A cross-toolchain produces machine code for a target ISA different from the development system.
Operating systems become useful as requirements for sharing, abstraction, coordination, protection and services grow.
The BVS1 system grows only when a new requirement motivates a new mechanism.

A useful test of understanding is to explain this complete path:
source code
    ↓
cross-toolchain
    ↓
RV64 executable
    ↓
QEMU program in the development VM
    ↓
emulated RV64 machine
    ↓
observable program behaviour
and then explain why successful execution still does not imply that the target contains an operating system.
crumbs: 1  From Executing Code to Operating Systems

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
text:
2.1 From source code to target-specific object code
Lecture 1 showed that an RV64 target can execute a small program without a guest operating system. Lecture 2 asks how that execution comes into existence and why, for an operating system, simply starting a program is not enough.
The path is:
and then:
The build tools are therefore not the final topic. We unfold them once because they make the transition from source code to a running machine state visible.
We first compile main.c without linking:
The important option is -c: stop before linking. The remaining options are course-provided target/build settings.
Inspecting the result with
shows that main.o is already a RISC-V ELF object.
ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) is the binary file format we use here for both object files and the final executable.
This distinction matters: the compiler has already translated C into code for our target ISA. The object file is therefore not architecture-neutral. But it is also not yet a complete program. Separate pieces can still refer to one another, and their final addresses have not yet been established.
The startup assembly is translated in the same way:
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
text:
mkdir -p build/manual

riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc -march=rv64imac -mabi=lp64 \
  -mcmodel=medany -msmall-data-limit=0 \
  -c main.c \
  -o build/manual/main.o


file build/manual/main.o




riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc -march=rv64imac -mabi=lp64 \
  -mcmodel=medany -c start.S -o build/manual/start.o
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
section: 2.2 Why object files still need a linker
text:
2.2 Why object files still need a linker
A symbol is a name used to refer to a program entity or location, such as a function or a linker-defined address.
Using nm (“name list”) lets us inspect the symbols in the two objects:
riscv64-unknown-elf-nm build/manual/start.o
riscv64-unknown-elf-nm build/manual/main.o
For the symbols relevant here, we can read the result as:
start.o defines _start
start.o needs   main
start.o needs   _stack_top

main.o  defines main
The important concept is not the letters printed by nm, but the relationship between separately translated pieces. One object can provide a symbol while another refers to it. The linker connects those pieces.
The unresolved _stack_top also reveals a second responsibility of the linker: it must establish where the program lives in target memory.
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
section: 2.3 From the stored-program idea to a concrete memory layout
text:
2.3 From the stored-program idea to a concrete memory layout
Lecture 1 used the abstract model:
instructions + data
        ↓
      memory
        ↕
       CPU
Our real program now contains different kinds of bytes that need concrete places.
The stack is runtime memory used during function calls, for example for local state and saved call information. The register sp is the stack pointer; _stack_top names the initial top address of this stack.
RV64 memory from 0x80000000

+----------------------------------------------------------+
| .text    _start, main, ...      | instructions          |
| .rodata  "Hello BVS1\n"         | constant data         |
| .data                           | initialized data      |
| .bss                            | zero-initialized data |
| C stack  (top: _stack_top)      | runtime data          |
+----------------------------------------------------------+
These roles are not properties that memory itself knows. They arise from the executable layout and from how the program and CPU use the addresses.
The course-provided linker.ld makes that layout concrete:
ENTRY(_start)

MEMORY {
    RAM (rwx) : ORIGIN = 0x80000000, LENGTH = 128M
}

. = ALIGN(16);
. += 16K;
_stack_top = .;
Here . is the linker’s current output address. After 16 KiB have been reserved for the initial stack, that address is named _stack_top.
Students do not need to write linker scripts in BVS1. The important idea is that the linker does not merely join files; it constructs one final arrangement of addresses in target memory in which the pieces can refer to one another.
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
section: 2.4 Linking produces the program QEMU can load
text:
2.4 Linking produces the program QEMU can load
We link the two objects using the course layout:
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc -nostdlib -nostartfiles -no-pie \
  -T linker.ld build/manual/start.o build/manual/main.o \
  -o build/manual/hello-bvs1.elf
Here -T linker.ld selects our course-provided memory layout; the remaining options are link settings for our target without a guest operating system.
At this point the linker has:

combined the objects;
resolved the symbol references;
established the final memory layout.

The resulting ELF is what QEMU receives. QEMU does not compile or link the program; it provides the emulated RV64 machine and loads the already-built image.
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
text:
2.5 Why execution starts before main
The linker script declares:
ENTRY(_start)
and _start is defined in start.S:
_start:
    la   sp, _stack_top
    call main
1:
    j    1b
This small fragment exposes an important boundary between machine startup and ordinary C code.
Before main can run, startup code establishes at least the execution environment that C expects. Here that means setting sp, the stack pointer, to the address denoted by _stack_top.
Then call main transfers control to main and remembers where execution should return. We deliberately do not open the full function-call mechanism yet. The fact that a return point must somehow be preserved becomes important in Lecture 3.
The local label 1: and 1b only express the final fallback loop: if main returns, execution remains there.
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
section: 2.6 The whole path, and what Make hides
text:
2.6 The whole path, and what Make hides
Running the ELF manually:
qemu-system-riscv64 -machine virt -m 128M \
  -smp 1 -nographic -bios none \
  -kernel build/manual/hello-bvs1.elf
reconstructs the complete path:
main.c    → compile  → main.o  ──┐
                                 │
start.S   → assemble → start.o ──┼─→ link → hello-bvs1.elf
                                 │                ↓
linker.ld ───────────────────────┘               QEMU
                                                  ↓
                                                 RV64
                                                  ↓
                                              Hello BVS1
Compilation, assembly, linking, and QEMU itself run in the Ubuntu development VM. The final RV64 instructions execute in the emulated target.
Make automates this workflow. It decides when a target is out of date and runs the corresponding recipe. The GCC driver performs the translation steps and invokes the linker. QEMU provides the machine on which the result executes.
Doing the path manually once is useful because the automation then has a visible meaning rather than being a black box.
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
section: 2.8 Why an executing program is not yet a process
text:
2.8 Why an executing program is not yet a process
Our current target has one execution:
_start
  ↓
main
  ↓
print
  ↓
for (;;) {}
Once it starts, nothing inside our target can currently stop it, regain control, and later continue it.
That is the new requirement. An operating system must be able to manage an execution rather than merely start it.
For our first model:

A process is an execution that the operating system can manage.

For Checkpoint 1, “manage” means only:
create → run → yield → resume → exit
This is intentionally much smaller than a complete Unix process model. We do not yet need address spaces, files, process IDs, or scheduling policies.
The minimum lifecycle is:
create ──→ READY ──run / resume──→ RUNNING ──exit──→ FINISHED
             ↑                       │
             └──────── yield ────────┘
A yielded process is still runnable. A finished process is not.
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
section: 2.10 The question that leads to execution context
text:
2.10 The question that leads to execution context
To resume correctly, something about the paused execution must survive:
process runs
     ↓
yield
     ↓
OS regains control
     ↓
resume
     ↓
continue exactly where it stopped
What must be preserved so this can work?
At this point it is enough to suspect that some machine state must survive the pause. Lecture 3 determines exactly what that state is.
The final path of Lecture 2 is therefore:
source → objects → linked ELF → memory → _start → main
followed by:
executing program → OS-managed execution → process
The remaining question is:

What machine state makes resume possible?
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes
text:
2.11 Key ideas
Lecture 2 connects the build path to the first process abstraction:

Compilation and assembly produce target-specific object files.
ELF is the binary format we use for both object files and the final executable.
Symbols name program entities or locations; the linker resolves references between separately translated pieces.
The linker also establishes the final memory layout of the program.
The stack is runtime memory used during function calls, and sp is the stack pointer.
Execution begins in startup code at _start, which establishes the initial environment before entering C.
QEMU loads the already-built ELF into the emulated RV64 target; it does not compile or link the program.
Make automates the build workflow, while the compiler, assembler, and linker perform the translation steps.
A process is an execution that the operating system can manage through create → run → yield → resume → exit.
yield and exit both return control to the operating system, but only a yielded execution may continue later.
Resuming means continuing where execution stopped, not restarting from the beginning.

A useful test of understanding is to explain both chains:
source → object files → linked ELF → memory → _start → main
and
executing program → OS-managed execution → process
and then explain why resuming a process requires some machine state to survive the pause.
crumbs: 2  From Source to Executables: Towards Processes

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.1 C pointer notation: a reminder
Lecture 2 ended with a requirement: run an execution, regain control, and continue that same execution later. Two questions follow: what must survive the pause, and how do we build that?
Our working definition is:
In BVS1, our minimal operating system will do the managing. For our first process, managing means:
This is the simplified lifecycle used for Checkpoint 1, rather than a general definition of every process’s lifetime. To stop and continue the same execution, our process needs an entry function, its own stack, saved CPU register state (its context), and lifecycle information: state and exit status.
This chapter builds those parts into one resumable execution. Creation prepares it without running its code; run starts or resumes it; yield returns control while preserving the ability to continue; exit finishes it.
The process representation will be a C struct. These expressions distinguish an object, its address, and a pointer to it:
Here p is the object, &p is its address, and q stores that address. In the declaration, * makes q a pointer; in an expression, *q dereferences the pointer to access the object.
p.state accesses the object’s state directly. (*q).state accesses the same member through the pointer; q->state is shorthand for that expression. The same notation lets us access a nested member such as q->context.sp once the context has been added.
For function pointers, storing a function and calling it are different operations:
In the assignment, worker converts to a pointer to that function, so the first line stores where to call. It does not call worker. The second line calls it through the stored pointer; worker() would call the function directly.

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.3 Understanding the process stack
The process needs owned stack storage: memory that remains associated with the process while the operating system executes elsewhere.
The process’s machine instructions are not copied onto that stack. They remain in the program’s .text section. The stack contains runtime data associated with active calls—for example saved register values, return information, some local variables, and temporary values when needed. Not every local variable is stored on the stack; the compiler may keep values in registers.
The array reserves storage; sp, the CPU’s stack-pointer register, selects the current position in that storage. Array indices increase toward higher addresses, while the RV64 C stack grows toward lower addresses:
                  stack grows this way
                         <-----

lower addresses                            higher addresses
&stack[0]               sp                &stack[STACK_SIZE]
    v                   v                           v
    +-----------------------------------------------+
    |                   | -- used stack ------------|
    +-----------------------------------------------+
&stack[STACK_SIZE] is the address just past the array’s last byte. A fresh process starts with an appropriately aligned sp at the high end; stack use then extends toward lower addresses. Reserving the array alone does not change the CPU’s active stack pointer.
Nested calls belong to the same execution and use the same process stack. For example:
void helper(int *x) { (*x)++; }
void worker(void) { int n = 1; helper(&n); }
Conceptually, while helper() is active:
                           sp
lower addresses            v               higher addresses
    +-----------------------------------------------+
    |             | helper frame | worker frame | - |
    +-----------------------------------------------+
The helper frame and worker frame labels denote runtime data associated with the active calls. The stack does not contain the machine instructions of helper() or worker(): the CPU executes those instructions from the .text section of the program’s memory layout.
The newer call uses space toward the lower-address end of the used stack. This is a schematic picture, not an exact compiler-generated layout: the compiler may inline calls or keep values in registers.
If the process yields from a nested call, that call chain’s stack data must remain intact while the OS uses its own stack. Resuming requires the process’s saved sp as well as the preserved storage.
crumbs: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.4 Continuation: where should execution return?
Lecture 2 showed the startup fragment:
call main
A RISC-V call remembers the location to which execution should later return. That location is stored in ra, the return-address register.
An ordinary return therefore already contains a useful idea:
call function
    |
    v
function executes
    |
    v
ret
    |
    v
continue at address stored in ra
If a process yields and is later resumed, the operating system must preserve some representation of the place where execution should continue. Preserving ra makes that idea concrete.
The stack data must survive too, and the process must recover the stack position recorded in sp. Restoring a continuation with the OS stack would not continue the same call chain.
crumbs: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.5 Context
At a pause, some execution state is still in CPU registers. Another execution can overwrite those values even when the process stack remains intact. The saved CPU register state needed to continue the execution is its context.
For the cooperative CP1 mechanism, the provided representation is:
struct context {
    uintptr_t ra;    // continuation address
    uintptr_t sp;    // current stack position
    uintptr_t s[12]; // saved s0 through s11
};
uintptr_t, defined by <stdint.h>, is an unsigned integer type, not a pointer type. It can hold the integer representation of a pointer value and later be converted back without losing that value. In our RV64 toolchain it is 64 bits wide. We use it for saved register-sized values such as ra and sp, which contain addresses during normal execution. Students are not expected to study the complete family of fixed-width integer types here.
The array s holds the RISC-V callee-saved registers s0 through s11: s[0] stores s0, through s[11] storing s11. A calling convention is the agreement that lets separately compiled functions cooperate about how registers are used. A callee-saved register is one whose value a called function must preserve for its caller. Preserving those required registers allows an ordinary C function call to cross the context-switch boundary safely.
Students do not need to memorize that register list or derive the complete assembly routine from the ABI. For CP1 they should be able to explain why ra and sp matter and why some additional register state must also survive.
crumbs: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
crumbs: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.7 The provided context-switch boundary
The course provides a function implemented in RISC-V assembly, with this C declaration:
void context_switch(
    struct context *current_context,
    const struct context *next_context);
current_context points to storage where the running execution’s registers will be saved. next_context points to the saved registers to restore. The const qualifier says the function does not modify the context object through next_context. Either context may belong to the OS execution or the process execution.
A context switch in this part of BVS1 means:

save the current execution context;
restore another saved context;
continue the restored execution.

The assembly below shows the matching save and restore operations. The ellipses stand for the corresponding operations on s1 through s10:
sd ra,    0(a0)
sd sp,    8(a0)
sd s0,   16(a0)
...
sd s11, 104(a0)

ld ra,    0(a1)
ld sp,    8(a1)
ld s0,   16(a1)
...
ld s11, 104(a1)

ret
sd (store doubleword) copies a 64-bit register value into memory; ld (load doubleword) copies a 64-bit value from memory into a register. In sd s0, 16(a0), the destination is the address in a0 plus 16 bytes. The offsets follow the context layout: ra at byte 0, sp at byte 8, and the twelve saved s registers at bytes 16 through 104.
After the loads, ret uses the newly restored ra. The switch therefore changes both the stack that is active and the location at which execution continues.
The stored fields and the restored fields match: ra, sp, and all twelve entries of s. The process needs both its stack memory and these saved register values to continue the same execution.
The function arguments current_context and next_context arrive in the RISC-V argument registers a0 and a1. These registers are caller-saved: their previous values are not part of the state that an ordinary C call promises to preserve. In this cooperative switch they are used to locate the two context structures; the persistent saved context is ra, sp, and s0-s11.
The same operation works in both directions:
OS running                         process running
    |                                   |
    | save OS context                   | save process context
    | restore process context           | restore OS context
    v                                   v
process running                       OS running
There is no scheduler here. CP1 contains only one process.

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.10 The lifecycle in C
Lecture 2 introduced:
create -> run -> yield -> resume -> exit
Lecture 3 now connects each semantic step to the minimum implementation work.

3.10.1 Create / prepare
Preparing a process means constructing a valid first-run state:
remember entry function
        |
choose process stack top
        |
prepare initial context
        |
state = READY
No process code has executed yet.
A process that has already yielded has a saved continuation. A new process does not.
The restore mechanism nevertheless expects a context containing a stack pointer and a continuation. The solution is to prepare an initial context before the process first runs.
Its initial stack pointer is placed at the aligned high end of its owned stack array.
The initial continuation is a small bootstrap function, called process_start(): an internal function used to enter a process for the first time. It is an implementation detail, not another public process operation.
Conceptually:
initial sp -> aligned high end of process.stack
initial ra -> process_start -> process.entry()
The first restore followed by ret therefore enters process_start() while using the process’s own stack.
process_start() calls the process entry function. If that function returns normally, process_start() calls process_exit(0). Returning from the entry function therefore finishes the process with status 0 and transfers control back to the OS.
Later resumes do not use the prepared bootstrap address again. A yield saves the real continuation from the running process, so the next restore continues after the context-switch call inside the yield path.
This is an important simplification:

First start and later resume use the same low-level restore mechanism.



3.10.2 Run and resume
The OS keeps a pointer named current_process to identify the process whose execution currently owns the CPU. process_yield() and process_exit() take no process argument: they use this pointer to find the object whose state and context they must update.
process_run(p) performs these steps:
reject p if its state is FINISHED
set current_process to p
set p's state to RUNNING
context switch from OS to p
The FINISHED check belongs to process_run(): a saved context does not by itself grant permission to run again.
The same run operation can support two cases:

a READY process that has never run starts through its prepared bootstrap context;
a READY process that yielded earlier resumes through the context saved by that yield.

The required behaviour is resume. A separate process_resume() API is not necessary.


3.10.3 Yield
For CP1:

yield means that the running process voluntarily returns control to the operating system while remaining able to resume later.

Using current_process, yield marks the process READY, saves its current context, and restores the OS context.
When the operating system later runs that process again, execution continues after the context-switch call inside the yield path.


3.10.4 Exit
For CP1:

exit means that the process finishes, records a result, and returns control to the operating system.

Using current_process, exit records the status in the process object, marks it FINISHED, and switches from the process context back to the OS context.
A finished process must not be resumed.
Yield and exit can use the same low-level control-transfer boundary, but their lifecycle meaning is different.
crumbs: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
crumbs: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.12 Why CP1 deliberately uses yield
CP1 needs a control transfer that gives the operating system control without finishing the process.
A timer interrupt would already introduce the preemption mechanism needed later for CP2. Blocking or sleeping would require an additional condition that makes the process runnable again. An ordinary C return would not expose the requirement to preserve and later restore a continuation.
A cooperative yield is therefore the smallest mechanism that makes resumability observable.
It also creates the next operating-system problem cleanly:

What if a process never yields?

That question motivates timer-driven preemption on the way to CP2.
crumbs: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.13 Check your model
Use these questions to check the distinction between restarting, resuming, and finishing:

What breaks if we call the entry function again after yield instead of restoring the saved context?
What breaks if we restore ra but not sp and s0-s11?
What breaks if process_run() allows a FINISHED process to execute again?

A successful explanation should connect each failure to the process representation: calling entry again restarts its work, restoring only part of the context cannot preserve the same execution, and restoring a finished process violates its lifecycle state.
crumbs: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue

title: 3  First Process: Stop and Continue
text:
3.14 Key ideas

A process is a managed execution.
Our process representation combines an entry function, owned stack storage, CPU context, lifecycle state, and exit status.
The stack is process-owned memory for the runtime data of active function calls. Function instructions remain in .text.
A context is the saved CPU register state needed to continue the same execution.
Lifecycle state says whether an execution may run; context says how it continues.
A context switch saves the current CPU register state and restores the next one. The same mechanism transfers control in both directions between OS and process.

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
text:
4.1 Locate editing, building, and execution
Lecture 3 constructed a process from an entry function, owned stack storage, saved CPU context, and lifecycle information. This chapter connects that abstraction to the machines and memory we actually use. It follows four questions raised by students: Where am I working? How do I edit the files that are actually built? Where is the program counter? Where do constants appear in the disassembly? Together they lead to the guiding question: where are our instructions and runtime data, and what must be preserved when execution pauses or is interrupted?
We use the same worker() and permute() from Exercise 2. The aim is to reconstruct and diagnose the existing mechanism before extending it.
Our setup has three machine roles:
The physical host supplies the outer infrastructure. Multipass manages the Ubuntu VM; it is not another machine layer. The VM is the development host for our tools. QEMU runs there as an ordinary Ubuntu process and emulates the target machine.
Both our OS-side control code and the managed process execute on the RV64 target. They do not become Ubuntu programs merely because QEMU runs in Ubuntu. The cross compiler and linker execute in the VM but generate an RV64 ELF for the target ISA.
The complete workflow is:
Make automates the build recipe. The editor changes source text; the compiler reads the saved file; QEMU receives the resulting ELF. An already running QEMU instance does not automatically acquire a new image when source files are edited or rebuilt.

text:
physical host: Linux / macOS / Windows
    |  hosts the VM; Multipass manages it
    v
Ubuntu VM bvs1: our development host
    |  runs editor, build tools, and QEMU
    v
QEMU emulates an RV64 target: CPU + RAM + UART
    |  target CPU executes RV64 instructions
    v
our program / growing BVS1 operating system



edit -> save source -> compile/link -> linked ELF
                                          |
                                 QEMU loads the image
                                          |
                                RV64 instructions execute

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
text:
4.2 Establish a reliable edit–build–run loop
Start on the physical host with:
multipass shell bvs1
Inside the VM, locate the existing repository and source file:
cd ~/teaching-bvs1-code
pwd
ls
nano main.c
Run make from the repository directory that contains the Makefile. Make reads the Makefile in the current directory, and that Makefile names the source files it compiles. A main.c edited in another directory or another copy of the repository is not this build’s input.
In nano, save with Ctrl-O, Enter, then leave with Ctrl-X. If using Vim, enter Insert mode with i, make the change, press Esc, then save and leave with :wq. The editor handout contains further details. The relevant competence is editing the intended file reliably; the choice of editor is not assessed.
After saving, inspect your change and build:
git diff -- main.c
make
make run
Use one small output-label change to connect the saved file to an observable effect. The array’s permutation should remain unchanged if only a label changes. End QEMU with Ctrl-a, release, then x. Restore that intentional label change before continuing.
If an old label appears, diagnose the chain in order:
saved source -> build input -> successful build -> executable -> QEMU run
Was the change saved? Is the saved file the one Make uses as build input? Did the build succeed and produce a new executable? Did a new QEMU session load that executable? Rebuilding repeatedly cannot correct an unsaved buffer or a different repository copy.

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
section: 4.4 Instructions and runtime data have different roles
text:
4.4 Instructions and runtime data have different roles
The linked program places machine instructions in .text. This includes instructions implementing the worker, helper, process API, and OS-side code. Calling a function transfers control to its instructions; it does not copy those instructions onto the stack.
The program counter, pc, identifies the instruction to execute. The stack pointer, sp, selects the current stack position. These are CPU state, not memory sections. A saved return address is an address value that points back into code; its being stored on the stack does not make the pointed-to instructions stack contents.
The stack holds runtime data associated with active calls: saved call information, saved registers, some local variables, and temporaries as needed. The labels worker frame and permute frame describe this runtime data, not the functions’ instructions.
A schematic snapshot after the first swap is:
.text                       process-owned stack storage
                            higher addresses
same worker instructions    +--------------------------+
same permute instructions   | worker: value V B S 1 \0 |
  ...                       +--------------------------+
  call process_yield        | permute call data        |
                            +--------------------------+
                            lower addresses
The CPU has changed data in the array while executing instructions that remain in .text. A non-inlined helper call uses the same process stack as the worker, with newer call data toward lower addresses. The picture does not prescribe exact offsets, compiler-generated frames, or a stack slot for every local value.
crumbs: 4  Where Our Code Runs

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
section: 4.5 sp, ra, and pc are different kinds of CPU state
text:
4.5 sp, ra, and pc are different kinds of CPU state
sp and ra are the conventional ABI names of the integer registers x2 and x1. Ordinary instructions read and write them like the other general-purpose registers x0–x31. The program counter is also architectural CPU state, but it is not one of these 32 registers. The CPU advances it as it executes, and jumps, branches, calls, and returns change it.
This explains why the Lecture 3 context contains ra, sp, and s0–s11 but no explicit pc. The cooperative context switch happens at an ordinary function-call boundary, so the saved ra already describes the continuation:
saved ra -> restored ra -> ret -> execution continues there
ret sets the program counter to the restored ra. The program counter is therefore not forgotten; the cooperative switch re-establishes it through ra.
crumbs: 4  Where Our Code Runs

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
section: 4.6 Follow the same execution through yield and resume
text:
4.6 Follow the same execution through yield and resume
When the process yields, the low-level switch saves its continuation, stack position, and required additional registers. The OS context is restored. The CPU’s current pc and sp now describe OS execution, while p.context holds the saved register values for the paused process. The array and suspended call data remain in p.stack.
The next process_run() restores that saved context. Low-level continuation first returns through the suspended yield path. process_yield() then returns to the same permute() invocation, which performs the second swap. The array becomes VB1S\0. The worker does not initialize it again, because no new worker invocation was started.
When the helper returns, the worker prints the result and calls process_exit(0). Exit marks the process FINISHED and returns control to the OS. Old bytes may physically remain after a helper returns or a process exits; that does not keep a call active or authorize another run. Lifecycle state determines whether the process may run again.



Moment
Array contents
CPU executes




worker initialized it
BVS1\0
process


first swap completed
VBS1\0
process


yielded
VBS1\0, preserved
OS


second swap completed
VB1S\0
process


process exited
no active array
OS



Calling entry again restarts the work; restoring a continuation without the matching stack position loses the original call chain; allowing a FINISHED process to run violates its lifecycle. These are different failures of the same model.
crumbs: 4  Where Our Code Runs

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
text:
4.7 Connect the other memory regions
The section names describe roles in the linked image:







Region
Role in our example




.text
RV64 machine instructions


.rodata
constant data, including output labels


.data
writable static/global objects with stored initial values, when present


.bss
zero-initialized static/global storage, including OS bookkeeping in the inspected library


OS stack
runtime data of OS-side calls


process stack storage
runtime data of the managed process’s calls



The output label "process: result: " is constant data, normally placed in .rodata. The initialized local value array is a separate writable object. Its C initializer does not put that array in .rodata: the compiler can provide its initial bytes from constants in instructions or from constant storage. Inspect the actual build rather than assuming a separate BVS1 string must be present in .rodata.
Constants therefore appear in the disassembly in two forms:

A value small enough to encode inside an instruction appears as an immediate operand, for example in li or addi. Larger values may be built by more than one instruction. The four characters of BVS1 can appear together as one 32-bit value: our target uses little-endian byte order, so storing 0x31535642 produces the bytes 0x42 0x56 0x53 0x31 at increasing addresses.
In this build, constant output labels are stored in .rodata. Instructions compute a label’s address, typically with an auipc/addi pair that objdump -d annotates with the resulting address, and pass it to uart_puts(). riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -s -j .rodata build/hello-bvs1.elf shows the bytes stored at that address.

For comparison, a static/global int initialized = 7 typically belongs to .data; a static/global int zeroed initially has value zero and typically belongs to .bss. Static storage lasts for the execution of the program, unlike the local state of a particular call. Neither declaration is needed in the Exercise 2 application merely to fill a diagram.
In the inspected Exercise 2 image, .data is empty. The local value array belongs to neither section: it lives on the process stack while worker() is active. Its .bss contains os_context and current_process from the provided library. A pointer becoming nonzero at runtime does not move its storage to .data. BSS occupies memory even though the ELF does not store all its initial zero bytes as file contents; loading/startup must establish the required initial state.
These roles do not imply that our minimal system enforces read/write permissions or separate address spaces. The course linker script and runtime storage choices determine the layout we are studying.

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
section: 4.9 Inspect the file without confusing it with live memory
text:
4.9 Inspect the file without confusing it with live memory
After a successful Exercise 2 build, run these commands in the VM:
riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -h build/hello-bvs1.elf
riscv64-unknown-elf-nm -n build/hello-bvs1.elf
riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -d \
  --disassemble=context_switch build/hello-bvs1.elf
The first command lists sections; the second lists symbols by address; the third decodes the selected function’s instructions. In nm, T/t identifies code symbols and B/b identifies BSS-related symbols. A symbol can simply name an address: _stack_top is the linker-defined initial OS-stack address, not a C array declaration. These inspection options are documented in the GNU Binutils manuals.
The commands inspect the ELF on disk. They do not display the running target’s CPU registers or the live contents of the local array. Debugging information can describe local variables, but that is different from a linker symbol or an observation of runtime memory.
The normal build uses -O2. It can inline permute(), meaning it incorporates the helper’s work into the caller instead of retaining a separate call. Local scalar values such as tmp can be kept in registers. The lecture’s separate observation build uses -O0 -g -fno-inline to retain inspectable function boundaries; -g adds debugging information. Exact frames and addresses depend on the build. See GCC’s Optimize Options.
crumbs: 4  Where Our Code Runs

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
section: 4.10 The next requirement: regain control without cooperation
text:
4.10 The next requirement: regain control without cooperation
Our current mechanism depends on the process reaching yield or exit. If it runs forever before either operation, our target-side OS continuation cannot run again. Ubuntu can still manage the QEMU process, but that is control at another layer. Terminating QEMU ends the target session rather than implementing target-side process management.
An interrupt signals an event. When enabled, it transfers control to a configured OS handler, allowing the OS to regain control. A future timer interrupt can make control transfer possible without a voluntary yield. This enables preemption: the OS takes control without the process’s cooperation. Scheduling then decides whether to continue the interrupted execution or select another runnable one. Interrupt handling and the scheduling decision are related but distinct steps.
This chapter raises that question without requiring an interrupt implementation for CP1. An arbitrary interruption is not an ordinary C call boundary. The interrupted continuation is not supplied by ra as it is at our cooperative call boundary; ra holds whatever value the interrupted code was using. The interrupted program counter must therefore be preserved explicitly, in dedicated trap state, together with the other registers the interrupted code may be using. The cooperative CP1 register subset is not by itself the full specification of such a mechanism.
crumbs: 4  Where Our Code Runs

title: 4  Where Our Code Runs
text:
4.11 Key ideas

The Ubuntu VM is our development host; the emulated RV64 machine is the target that executes our program’s instructions.
Editing, saving, building, and starting a new run are separate steps in one observable workflow.
Function instructions remain in .text; stack frames contain runtime data associated with active calls.
A local writable array is distinct from constant data used to initialize it or print an output label.
Process stack storage is an array in the process object; its role does not prescribe an ELF section or an address space.
Preserved stack data and saved register context together support continuing the same execution.
The program counter is CPU state but not a general-purpose register: the cooperative switch re-establishes it through ra and ret, whereas an interruption must preserve it explicitly.
Lifecycle state determines whether another run is permitted, even if old memory contents remain.
